title: The letter to Diognetus
hookLine: Christians live in every country, as the soul lives in the body

cards: A man named Diognetus has questions about the Christians. Who is this God they trust? Why do they look down on death, and refuse the gods of the Greeks?
What is this love they have for one another? And why did this new way of living show up now, and not long ago? Someone writes him an answer.
Nobody knows who wrote it, or who Diognetus was. The letter has no signature and no date. But its description of Christians would one day be quoted by a council of the Church.

teach.b: First, the writer says, Christians look ordinary. They aren't marked off by country, language or customs. They don't live in cities of their own, or speak some odd dialect.
They follow the local ways in clothes and food and daily life. Second, the paradox. They live in their own countries, but as visitors.
Every foreign country is a homeland to them, and every homeland is foreign. They marry and have children like everyone else, but they don't abandon their babies. They share their table.
They obey the laws, and in their own lives go further than the laws ask. They love all people, the letter says, and all people persecute them. Third, the picture behind today's line.
In Lightfoot's translation: "In a word, what the soul is in a body, this the Christians are in the world."
The soul is spread through every part of the body; Christians through the cities of the world. The soul lives in the body but isn't of the body; Christians live in the world but aren't of the world.
The soul is unseen, but it holds the body together, and the writer says Christians hold the world together in the same quiet way. Fourth, why Catholics still read it.
The Second Vatican Council borrowed the line for the calling of lay Catholics: what the soul is in the body, let Christians be in the world.

teach.h: WHAT THE SOUL IS IN A BODY.
teach.b: Not a separate town. Not a fortress. Ordinary streets, ordinary jobs, ordinary food, and something inside that keeps the whole thing alive.
It's a big claim, and the letter makes it calmly, as a description, to a stranger who simply asked.

how: Catholic teaching describes the calling of lay people as living the faith inside ordinary work, family and civic life, and the Second Vatican Council quoted the letter to Diognetus to say so.

practice: Picture the people who live or work nearest you, known by name or only by a nod, and let one of them come forward.
What would make their week a little lighter: taking in a package, a note, an offer to help, something small enough that nobody needs to know? If you pray, hold that neighbor before God.
